title: The Date on Your Food: What "Best Before" and "Use By" Really Say (and What They Don't)
format: 16:9 animated, paper A4 style, long form (~8:30)
parts: Is the date on your food a warning, or just a suggestion?
Two dates. Same pack, same tiny print. In Europe, one is about quality and one is about safety. In America? The same words can mean something else.
Mix them up, and you can waste good food, or miss the one date that is about safety.
So why does food have two dates? And who decided?
Let us follow the evidence. Welcome to The Everyday Mystery.
Open your cupboard. Pick up a bag of pasta. Now open the fridge, and pick up a pack of fresh meat.
The pasta says best before. The fresh meat says use by.
They look like twins. They are not.
Here is the deal for this video. We repeat what food agencies, laws and named organizations say, and we tell you who said it. Anything that is our own reading, we label as ours.
And one note. This is not medical advice. For any real food, read the label and its storage instructions.
Let us start with the people who wrote the rules. In Europe, food agencies treat them as two very different messages.
Here is how the European Food Safety Authority explains use by. Foods can be eaten until this date but not after, even if they look and smell fine.
And best before, in its words: the food will be safe to eat after this date but may not be at its best.
That is the whole idea in two sentences. Use by is a safety line. Best before is a quality line.
One more detail, from the same agencies: both dates only count if the food is kept the way the label says.
So why does a safety line need a date at all? Because of what you cannot see. The European authority's consumer page says harmful bacteria you cannot see or smell might make you ill.

European law has a word for it: microbiological. For foods that are highly perishable from a microbiological point of view, the use by date replaces the best before date. And after a use by date, the law says, the food is deemed unsafe.
Spain's food agency agrees, and gives examples. Best before goes on flour, rice, pasta, biscuits, canned food, oil and honey. Use by goes on fresh meat or fish.
So who picks the label? Food businesses do.

The European authority built a decision tool to help them choose. It asks questions. Does the law already set rules for this kind of food? Does the product get a treatment that removes hazards? Is it handled before it is packed? And what is the product like, and how is it stored?
Behind the label, the authority says, food safety scientists and producers work together to keep the dates accurate.
And in twenty eleven, the British government gave its own rule of thumb: use by only where food could be unsafe after that date.
Its examples for use by: soft cheese, ready-prepared meals and smoked fish. For best before: biscuits, jam, pickles, crisps and tinned food.
So the label is not a mood. It is a choice, made by the business, against a safety question.
But where did dates come from? There are three obvious guesses.
One: governments invented them to protect us. Two: scientists found the one exact day each food goes off. Three: a shop wanted tidier shelves.
Let us test the third. According to The Spectator, the story starts with the British store Marks and Spencer, in the nineteen fifties.
They printed dates on food, but only for use in the stockroom.
By nineteen seventy, the dates were on the shelves. The store says that was several years before dates became compulsory.
In nineteen seventy-three, it named them sell-by dates.
Other supermarkets soon followed, The Spectator says, after evidence that shoppers liked the reassurance of a date.
Then, The Spectator says, came the two labels we know today. It calls best before advisory, and use by a sign of a genuine risk of food poisoning.
That is one account, not a government archive. Our reading: it suggests dates began as a store tool.
And that store tool left a mark. In twenty eleven, the British government asked for sell-by and display-until labels to be removed, because they were used for stock rotation and confused shoppers.
So of our three guesses, the third has the best evidence we found. Science helps, and rules did come later. But the shelf came first.
And there is a third date: sell by. Is that one about safety, too?
In its published guidance, the United States Department of Agriculture says a sell-by date tells the store how long to display a product. It is not a safety date.
It also says that, except for infant formula, federal rules do not require product dates.
For meat, poultry and egg products, it says dates may be added voluntarily, as long as they are truthful and not misleading.
And here is the twist. In that guidance, use by means peak quality, not safety, except on infant formula.
In Europe, use by is the safety date. Same words, different meaning.
Our reading: that is how the same two words can send you the wrong way, the moment you cross a border.
In twenty nineteen, the American Food and Drug Administration wrote to the food industry with a request: use one phrase for quality dates. Best if used by.

The agency pointed to an estimate that confusion over date labels accounts for about twenty percent of food waste in American homes. The Department of Agriculture's guidance also recommends best if used by for quality dates.
So the sensible habit is simple: check what the label means in the country where you shop.
But there is one more date on some packs, and it was never meant for you.
Turn over some tins and you may find a jumble of letters and numbers. What are they?
The United States Department of Agriculture calls it closed dating: a code that identifies when the product was made.
It has a job. The guidance says cans must carry a packing code, so manufacturers can rotate their stock, and find their products if there is a recall.
So one tin can carry two dates: one for you, and one for the factory. Our reading: the factory code is not for shoppers. Its job is rotating stock and finding products in a recall.
Now the opposite. Does every food need a date? In Europe, the law says no, and it says which ones.
The list in the regulation includes fresh fruit and vegetables that have not been peeled or cut. Vinegar. Cooking salt. Solid sugar. Chewing gum. Drinks with ten percent alcohol or more.
Bakers' wares are on the list too, with a reason: they are normally eaten within twenty-four hours.
Eggs are an odd one. Food Standards Scotland says the best before date on eggs is set at no more than twenty-eight days after laying.
And the UK government's guidance for caterers says it plainly: do not use eggs beyond their best before date. That page is written for businesses serving the public.

Here is the part that costs money. First, do people understand all this? Not as well as you would hope. In a two thousand fifteen survey for the European Commission, forty-seven percent said they understood best before. For use by, forty percent. And almost half of the people asked wanted clearer information.
Why does any of this matter? Waste.
In twenty twenty, the European authority wrote that the European Commission estimates up to ten percent of food waste in the EU is linked to date marking.
Linked, not caused. And it is an estimate.

In Britain, the waste organisation WRAP estimates that around one hundred and eighty thousand tonnes of food, worth about five hundred million pounds, are thrown away from homes every year, linked to best before dates.
WRAP's review, using twenty fifteen data, says date labels are cited as a factor in about a third of the roughly two million tonnes of household food thrown away because it was not used in time.
That is why WRAP told businesses and food redistribution groups to look again at food past its best before date. But, it said, no food should be sold, redistributed or eaten after the use by.
Our reading: a date can be two things at once. A useful safety line, and a source of waste when we read the quality line as if it were the safety line.

And the story has come full circle. In twenty twenty-two, The Spectator noted that Marks and Spencer said it was dropping sell-by dates on many fruits and vegetables, and going back to stockroom codes.
From the stockroom, to the shelf, and back to the stockroom.
So what do you actually do at the shelf? Not medical advice, only how to read a label.
One: find the exact words on the pack. Use by and best before are not the same message.
Two: read the storage instructions. The European authority's decision tool takes storage into account, and the UK government says poor storage can make food unsafe before the date.

Three: freezing. Spain's food agency says that before a food reaches its use-by date, you can freeze it at home to keep it longer. And the UK government says defrosted food should be used within twenty-four hours.
Four: on a use by food, looking and sniffing is not a test. The European authority says food can look and smell fine.
If you are unsure, follow the label and your national food agency, not a guess.

So let us count. The two dates, as the agencies define them: documented. Dates starting in a store: one account, so only partly. Governments inventing them: not what that account says. The rules did come, and today they define use by.
So the two dates are really two questions. Is it safe? And is it at its best?
Use by answers the first. Best before answers the second.
So here is a last question for the dinner table. Which date in your kitchen did you never really understand?
